findings.title: Double free / double drop of elements when a destructor panics during IntoIter drop
findings.evidence: impl<T> Drop for IntoIter<T> (src/lib.rs:2539-2556) moves the buffer into a temporary owning local (line 2546, mem::replace(&mut this.vec, ThinVec::new())), drops the not-yet-yielded elements with ptr::drop_in_place(&mut vec[this.start..]) (line 2547), and only afterwards shrinks the length with vec.set_len_non_singleton(0) (line 2548). The length is not reset before the drop call and vec is an owning ThinVec local, so if any remaining elements destructor panics, the slice drop-glue drops the rest of the elements and then unwinding drops the vec local, running ThinVec::drop -> drop_non_singleton (src/lib.rs:1915-1924) over the still-full [..] slice: every element in [start, len) is destroyed a second time (double free / use-after-free) and the already-moved-out elements in [0, start) are destroyed too. Reachable from fully safe user code: any T whose Drop impl can panic, e.g. let v = thin_vec![Bad(1), Bad(0xbadbeef), Bad(3)]; drop(v.into_iter()); where Bad::drop panics. Contrast ThinVec::truncate (src/lib.rs:1055-1066), which deliberately calls set_len_non_singleton(new_len) BEFORE drop_in_place so a panicking destructor cannot re-drop the value; IntoIter::drop omits that guard. Reproduced locally against this exact source: a 3-element IntoIter whose middle element panics once on drop runs the element destructors a second time (observed call stack IntoIter::drop::drop_non_singleton -> ThinVec::drop::drop_non_singleton), and a String-owning variant aborts with STATUS_HEAP_CORRUPTION (0xC0000374), a real heap double-free/heap-corruption primitive from safe code.
